en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the Buddha, concerning the Question on Inference.
3. The Question on the Right Practice of Laypeople and Those Who Have Gone Forth “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, I praise the right practice of either a layperson or one who has gone forth; whether it be a layperson, monks,’” [and so on].
“Or one who has gone forth, practicing rightly, through the cause of that right practice, becomes an attainer of the true method, the Dhamma, and the wholesome. “If,
venerable Nāgasena, a householder clad in white, enjoying sensual pleasures, dwelling in a bed crowded with children and wife,
using Kāsī cloth and sandalwood, wearing garlands, scents, and ointments, and accepting gold and silver— ”
One who has bound on a head-dress variegated with jeweled earrings, practicing rightly, becomes an achiever of the noble, wholesome Dhamma; likewise, even one who has gone forth,
clothed in shaven-garment robes of saffron, dependent on alms from others, perfectly fulfilling the four aggregates of virtue,
conducting himself having undertaken the one hundred and fifty training rules, and [observing] the thirteen ascetic qualities...
"One who practices without remainder and is rightly established is a successful achiever of the method, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.
In that regard, venerable sir, what is the distinction between a householder and one who has gone forth?
The practice of asceticism is fruitless; the going forth is useless."

“Barren is the guarding of the training rules; fruitless is the undertaking of the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa). What is the point of practicing suffering there? Is it not indeed the case that happiness is to be attained through happiness itself?
“It was indeed spoken thus, Great King, by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, I praise the right practice of both the householder and the one gone forth. Whether it be a householder, monks, or...”
"Whether one has gone forth or not, it is the one who practices rightly who, by reason of that right practice, succeeds in attaining the true way, the Dhamma, and the wholesome.

Thus it is, Great King: only the one who practices rightly is best. Even one who has gone forth, Great King, if he does not practice rightly thinking "I have gone forth," is far indeed from the state of a recluse and far indeed from the state of a brahmin, let alone a householder clad in white.

"Great King, a householder who practices rightly is successful in the noble Dhamma that is wholesome; and a renunciant, Great King, who practices rightly is also successful in the noble Dhamma that is wholesome.
Nevertheless, Great King, it is the renunciant alone who is the master and lord of the state of a recluse (sāmañña).
Renunciation, Great King, possesses many virtues, manifold virtues, immeasurable virtues; it is not possible to set a limit to the virtues of renunciation."
“Just as, great king, it is not possible by means of wealth to determine the value or measure of a wish-fulfilling gem, saying, ‘The price of this gem is this much’;
even so, great king, the going-forth has many virtues, manifold virtues, immeasurable virtues—it is not possible to determine the measure of the virtue of the going-forth.
Or again, great king, just as it is not possible to determine the measure of the waves in the great ocean, saying, ‘There are this many waves in the great ocean’;”
In the same way, Great King, the going forth has many virtues, manifold virtues, immeasurable virtues; it is not possible to measure the virtue of the going forth.
Whatever task is to be done by one who has gone forth, Great King, all that succeeds quickly and not after a long time.
For what reason?
“Great King, one who has gone forth is of few wishes, contented, secluded, unattached, energetic,
without abode, homeless, perfect in virtue, refined in conduct, and skilled in the practice of the ascetic virtues (dhutaṅga).
For that reason, whatever task a person who has gone forth has to do, all of it succeeds quickly and not after a long time.”
“Just as, O Great King, a straight, stainless, and well-polished arrow, free from knots, flies true when well-aimed;
even so, O Great King, whatever task is to be done by one who has gone forth succeeds quickly and not after a long time.
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; I accept it as you have said.”
The third question: on the right practice of householders and those who have gone forth.
